{{Short description|Theorem on finite linear groups}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Jordan–Schur theorem''' also known as '''Jordan's theorem on finite linear groups''' is a theorem in its original form due to [[Camille Jordan]]. In that form, it states that there is a [[function (mathematics)|function]] ''ƒ''(''n'') such that given a finite [[subgroup]] ''G'' of the [[group (mathematics)|group]] {{nowrap|GL(''n'', '''C''')}} of [[invertible matrix|invertible]] ''n''-by-''n'' [[complex number|complex]] [[matrix (mathematics)|matrices]], there is a subgroup ''H'' of ''G'' with the following properties:

* ''H'' is [[Abelian group|abelian]].
* ''H'' is a [[normal subgroup]] of ''G''.
* The index of ''H'' in ''G'' satisfies (''G'' : ''H'')&nbsp;≤&nbsp;''ƒ''(''n'').

[[Issai Schur|Schur]] proved a more general result that applies when ''G'' is not assumed to be finite, but just [[Periodic group|periodic]]. Schur showed that ''ƒ''(''n'') may be taken to be 
:((8''n'')<sup>1/2</sup>&nbsp;+ 1)<sup>2''n''<sup>2</sup></sup>&nbsp;−&nbsp;((8''n'')<sup>1/2</sup>&nbsp;− 1)<sup>2''n''<sup>2</sup></sup>.<ref name="Curtis">{{cite book |title=Representation Theory of Finite Groups and Associative Algebras |last1=Curtis |first1=Charles | author1-link = Charles W. Curtis  |last2=Reiner|first2= Irving|author2-link=Irving Reiner |year=1962 |publisher=John Wiley & Sons |pages=258–262}}</ref>

A tighter bound (for ''n''&nbsp;≥&nbsp;3) is due to [[Andreas Speiser|Speiser]], who showed that as long as ''G'' is finite, one can take 
:''ƒ''(''n'')&nbsp;=&nbsp;''n''! 12<sup>''n''(''π''(''n''+1)+1)</sup>

where ''π''(''n'') is the [[prime-counting function]].<ref name="Curtis"/><ref name=Speiser>{{cite book|last=Speiser|first=Andreas|title=Die Theorie der Gruppen von endlicher Ordnung, mit Anwendungen auf algebraische Zahlen und Gleichungen sowie auf die Krystallographie, von Andreas Speiser|year=1945|publisher=Dover Publications|location=New York|pages=216–220}}</ref>  This was subsequently improved by [[Hans Frederick Blichfeldt]] who replaced the 12 with a 6. Unpublished work on the finite case was also done by [[Boris Weisfeiler]].<ref name=Collins>{{cite journal|last=Collins|first=Michael J.|title=On Jordan's theorem for complex linear groups|journal=Journal of Group Theory|year=2007|volume=10|issue=4|pages=411–423|doi=10.1515/JGT.2007.032}}</ref> Subsequently, [[Michael J. Collins|Michael Collins]], using the [[classification of finite simple groups]], showed that in the finite case, one can take ''ƒ''(''n'')&nbsp;=&nbsp;(''n'' + 1)! when ''n'' is at least 71, and gave near complete descriptions of the behavior for smaller ''n''.


==Generalization to arbitrary fields==
The theorem has also been extended to finite subgroups of general linear groups over arbitrary fields - with a more complicated albeit analogous statement - by Collins<ref name=Collins2>{{cite journal|last=Collins|first=Michael J.|title=Modular analogues of Jordan's theorem for finite linear groups|journal=J. Reine Angew. Math.|year=2008|volume=624|pages=143-171|doi=10.1515/CRELLE.2008.084|arxiv=0709.3245}}</ref> and separately Larsen and Pink.<ref name=LarsenPink>{{cite journal|last1=Larsen|first1=Michael J.|last2=Pink|first2=Richard|title=Finite subgroups of algebraic groups|journal=J. Amer. Math. Soc.|year=2011|volume=24|issue=4|pages=1105-1158|doi=10.1090/S0894-0347-2011-00695-4}}</ref> Collins's paper includes exact bounds and depends on the [[classification of finite simple groups]]; Larsen and Pink used a different approach that avoids depending on the CFSG.
